title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk-iso}
		In the algebraic setting, the role of the Atiyah extension $A(E)$ is played by the sheaf $\mathcal D^1(E)$ of scalar differential operators of order at most one on $E$ (see \cite{Ser06} for the line bundle case and \cite{Mar09} for the general case). Recall that a \textit{differential operator of order $1$} on a holomorphic vector bundle $E$ of rank $r$ is a linear map $P\colon \Omega^0(E)\to \Omega^0(E)$ which, locally, takes the form
		\[
		P = (g_{ij}) + \sum_{k=1}^n (h_{ij}^k) \frac{\partial}{\partial z^k},
		\]
		where $(g_{ij})$ and $(h_{ij}^k)$ are $r\times r$ matrices of holomorphic functions. Such an operator is said to have \textit{scalar principal symbol} if $(h_{ij}^k) = h^k \cdot \mathrm I_{r\times r}$ for some local holomorphic functions $h^k$. There exists an exact sequence
		\[
		0 \longrightarrow \operatorname{End}E \longrightarrow \mathcal D^1(E) \xrightarrow[\quad\,]{\sigma} T_X^{1,0} \longrightarrow 0,
		\]
		where the symbol map $\sigma$ is locally given by $\sigma(P)=\sum_{k=1}^n h^k \frac{\partial}{\partial z_k}$. It was shown in e.g. \cite[Proposition A.2]{CS16} that $\mathcal D^1(E)$ carries a natural holomorphic structure, under which it is isomorphic to the Atiyah extension $A(E)$. Therefore, the DGLA $(A^{0,\bullet}(X,A(E)), \bar\partial_{A(E)}, [\cdot,\cdot])$ above is naturally isomorphic to the one obtained via the algebraic construction.

label: prop:formal-vs-canonical
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:formal-vs-canonical}
		The joint deformations of   $(X,E)$ are unobstructed  if and only if for $\epsilon_1(t)$ defined in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[e1]{(\ref*{e1})}},
		the   obstruction equation
		\[
		\bar\partial_{A(E)}\epsilon(t)
		=
		\frac12\,[\epsilon(t),\epsilon(t)],
		\]
		or equivalently, writing $\epsilon(t) = (A_t,\varphi_t)$, 
		\begin{empheq}[left=\empheqlbrace]{align}
			\bar{\partial}\varphi_t &= \frac{1}{2}[\varphi_t,\varphi_t];  \tag{MC1}\label{MC1} \\[6pt]
			\bar{\partial}_{\operatorname{End} E} A_t &= \varphi_t \lrcorner R_E + \varphi_t \lrcorner D_{\operatorname{End} E}^{1,0} A_t - \frac{1}{2}[A_t,A_t] \tag{MC2}\label{MC2},
		\end{empheq}
		can be solved order-by-order formally.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The “only if’’ part is clear by setting $\epsilon(t):=\epsilon^{\mathrm{can}}(t)$ as in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[good]{(\ref*{good})}}.
		
		For the converse, the degree-two  part of the Maurer--Cartan equation reads
		\[
		\bar\partial_{A(E)}\epsilon_2(t)
		=
		\frac{1}{2}\,[\epsilon_1(t),\epsilon_1(t)].
		\]
		In particular, $[\epsilon_1(t),\epsilon_1(t)]$ is $\bar\partial_{A(E)}$-exact. By bundle-valued Hodge decomposition,
		\[
		[\epsilon_1(t),\epsilon_1(t)]
		=
		\mathcal H[\epsilon_1(t),\epsilon_1(t)]
		+
		\bar\partial_{A(E)}\bar\partial_{A(E)}^*\mathcal G[\epsilon_1(t),\epsilon_1(t)]
		+
		\bar\partial_{A(E)}^*\bar\partial_{A(E)}\mathcal G[\epsilon_1(t),\epsilon_1(t)],
		\]
		and exactness forces $\mathcal H[\epsilon_1(t),\epsilon_1(t)]=0$, hence
		\[
		[\epsilon_1(t),\epsilon_1(t)]
		=
		\bar\partial_{A(E)}\bar\partial_{A(E)}^*\mathcal G[\epsilon_1(t),\epsilon_1(t)].
		\]
		We then replace $\epsilon_2(t)$ by the degree-two term of the canonical solution of \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[good]{(\ref*{good})}}, namely
		\[
		\epsilon_2^{\mathrm{can}}(t)
		=
		\frac{1}{2}\,\bar\partial_{A(E)}^*\mathcal G[\epsilon_1(t),\epsilon_1(t)]
		\]
		presented in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[epsilon2]{(\ref*{epsilon2})}}, which  still solves the  Maurer--Cartan equation in degree-two.
		
		\medskip
	At each higher order $N \ge 3$, a slightly more involved
	argument shows that one may replace $\epsilon_N(t)$ by
	the ``better'' term $\epsilon_N^{\mathrm{can}}(t)$, so that
	the full (convergent) power series $\epsilon^{\mathrm{can}}(t)$
	as in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[good]{(\ref*{good})}} still satisfies the Maurer--Cartan equation
	over a sufficiently small disc. This yields the desired
	unobstructedness.

label: step1
title: Proof
body_md:
The proof  will be divided into two steps.
		\begin{step}{Reduction on the obstruction equations:   Calabi--Yau property \& assumption $H^2(X,\operatorname{End} ^0 E)=0$.}\label{step1}
		\end{step}
		
		Under the assumption that $K_X$ is torsion, i.e., $lK_X$ is holomorphically trivial for some integer $l\geq  1$, write
		\begin{equation} \label{bundle F}
			lK_X = K_X + (l-1)K_X \quad \text{and set} \quad F := (l-1)K_X.
		\end{equation}
		Since $F$ is also torsion, it is  Hermitian  flat. More precisely, we can equip $F$ with a Hermitian metric $h_F$ whose Chern connection $$\nabla_F = D_F^{1,0} + \bar\partial_F$$ is flat, meaning its curvature $R_F$ vanishes.
		
		Moreover, there exists a nowhere vanishing $F$-valued holomorphic $(n,0)$-form
		\[
		\boldsymbol{\Omega} \in H^0(X, lK_X) \simeq H^{n,0}(X, F).
		\]
		
		
		
		We will need the following bundle-valued version of the Tian--Todorov lemma, in which the flatness of $F$ is not required --- it will be needed  later; see Lemma \ref{Fujiki}.
		
		\begin{lemma}[{\cite[Corollary 3.4]{LR12}}]\label{Tian-Todorov}
			For any $\varphi,\psi\in A^{0,1}\bigl(X, T_X^{1,0}\bigr)$ and any $\eta\in A^{\bullet,\bullet}(X,F)$, one has
			\[
			[\varphi,\psi] \lrcorner \eta
			= -D_F^{1,0}\bigl(\psi \lrcorner \bigl(\varphi \lrcorner \eta\bigr)\bigr)
			+ \psi \lrcorner D_F^{1,0}\bigl(\varphi \lrcorner \eta\bigr)
			+ \varphi \lrcorner D_F^{1,0}\bigl(\psi \lrcorner \eta\bigr)-\psi \lrcorner\bigl(\varphi\lrcorner D_F^{1,0} \eta\bigr)
			\]
		\end{lemma}
		
		
		
		Using the Calabi--Yau property of $X$ and following the insightful idea dating back to \cite{LRW19}  (also developed in \cite{Zha26}), we will need another auxiliary formal power series $\Omega(t)$ with $\Omega(0)=\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ to further reduce Proposition \ref{prop:formal-vs-canonical}   to the following:
		
		\begin{proposition}\label{prop-1}
			In the setting of Theorem  \ref{main thm},     for any first-order deformation 
			$\epsilon_1=(A_1,\varphi_1)$, suppose that there exist formal power series
			\[
			\varphi(t)=\sum_{i\geq 1}\varphi_i t^i \in A^{0,1}(X, T_X^{1,0})[[t]],\quad
			a(t)=\sum_{i\geq 1} a_i t^i  \in A^{0,1}(X,\mathcal O_X)[[t]], \quad a_1=\operatorname{tr} A_1,
			\]
			and
			\[
			\Omega(t)=\Omega_0+\sum_{i\geq 1}\Omega_i t^i\in A^{n,0}(X, F)[[t]],\quad	\Omega_0=\boldsymbol{\Omega},
			\]
			satisfying the system formally:
			\begin{equation}\tag{$\dagger$}\label{log 0.2}
				\begin{cases}
					\bigl(\bar\partial_F + D_F^{1,0}\circ \varphi(t)\lrcorner\bigr)\Omega(t)=0,\\[0.8em]
					\bigl(\bar\partial_F + \dfrac{1}{2}D_F^{1,0}\circ \varphi(t)\lrcorner\bigr)\bigl(\varphi(t)\lrcorner\Omega(t)\bigr)=0,\\[0.8em]
					\Bigl(		\bar\partial a(t)-\varphi(t) \lrcorner \operatorname{tr} R_E- \varphi(t)\lrcorner \partial a(t)\Bigr)\wedge\Omega(t)=0.\\
				\end{cases}
			\end{equation}
			Then the Kuranishi space of the pair $(X,E)$ is smooth.
		\end{proposition}
		
		\begin{proof}
			The first two 	equations in  \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.2]{(\ref*{log 0.2})}} together with Lemma \ref{Tian-Todorov} (noting that $\Omega(t)$ is automatically $D_F^{1,0}$-closed for type reasons) imply
			\begin{align*}
				\bar\partial\bigl(\varphi(t)\lrcorner \Omega(t)\bigr)
				&= -\frac{1}{2}\,D^{1,0}_F\Bigl(\varphi(t)\lrcorner\bigl(\varphi(t)\lrcorner\Omega(t)\bigr)\Bigr)\\
				&= \frac{1}{2}\,[\varphi(t),\varphi(t)]\lrcorner \Omega(t)
				- \varphi(t)\lrcorner D^{1,0}_F\bigl(\varphi(t)\lrcorner\Omega(t)\bigr)\\
				&= \frac{1}{2}\,[\varphi(t),\varphi(t)]\lrcorner \Omega(t)
				+ \varphi(t)\lrcorner\bar\partial\Omega(t).
			\end{align*}
			Hence
			\begin{equation}\label{aabb}
				\bigl(\bar\partial\varphi(t)\bigr)\lrcorner \Omega(t)
				= \bar\partial\bigl(\varphi(t)\lrcorner \Omega(t)\bigr)
				- \varphi(t)\lrcorner\bar\partial\Omega(t)
				= \frac{1}{2}\,[\varphi(t),\varphi(t)]\lrcorner \Omega(t).
			\end{equation}
			
			Set 
			\[
			V(t) := \bar\partial\varphi(t) - \frac{1}{2}[\varphi(t),\varphi(t)] = \sum_{i\ge 2} v_i t^i,
			\]
			with \(v_i \in A^{0,2}(X,T_X^{1,0})\). Then \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[aabb]{(\ref*{aabb})}} becomes \(V(t)\lrcorner\Omega(t)=0\).
			
			Locally write 
			\[
			\boldsymbol{\Omega} = f(z)\,dz^1\wedge\cdots\wedge dz^n\otimes e
			\]
			with \(f(z)\) nowhere vanishing and \(e\) a local frame of \(F\). Any \(v\in A^{0,2}(X,T_X^{1,0})\) can be expressed locally as
			\[
			v = \sum_{j=1}^n g_j\,\frac{\partial}{\partial z^j},
			\quad\text{where } g_j \text{ are smooth }(0,2)\text{-forms}.
			\]
			Contracting with \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) gives
			\[
			\boldsymbol{\Omega}\lrcorner v = f(z)\sum_{j=1}^n (-1)^{j-1} g_j\,
			dz^1\wedge\cdots\wedge\widehat{dz^j}\wedge\cdots\wedge dz^n\otimes e.
			\]
			The \((n-1,2)\)-forms appearing are linearly independent, hence the map \(v\mapsto\boldsymbol{\Omega}\lrcorner v\) is injective.
			
			
			\medskip
			Expanding
			\[
			V(t)\lrcorner\Omega(t)=\sum_{k\ge 2}\Bigl(\sum_{i+j=k}v_i\lrcorner\Omega_j\Bigr)t^k=0,
			\]
			we obtain:
			
			\begin{itemize}	\setlength{\itemsep}{5pt}
				\item[$\centerdot$] For \(k=2\), \(v_2\lrcorner\boldsymbol{\Omega}=0\), so \(v_2=0\) by injectivity.
				\item[$\centerdot$] Assume \(v_2=\dots=v_{N}=0\) for some \(N\ge 2\). Then the coefficient of \(t^{N+1}\) reduces to \(v_{N+1}\lrcorner\boldsymbol{\Omega}=0\), hence \(v_{N+1}=0\).
			\end{itemize}
			Therefore  \(V(t)=0\), i.e., 
			\begin{equation}\label{hhh}
				\bar\partial\varphi(t) = \dfrac{1}{2}[\varphi(t),\varphi(t)],
			\end{equation}
			namely the first obstruction equation \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[MC1]{(\ref*{MC1})}}.
			
			
			\medskip
			\medskip
			Via a similar argument, the third equation in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.2]{(\ref*{log 0.2})}} is equivalent to 
			\begin{equation}
				\bar\partial a(t)=\varphi(t) \lrcorner \operatorname{tr} R_E+ \varphi(t)\lrcorner \partial a(t).
			\end{equation}
			This is obtained by taking the trace of the second obstruction equation \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[MC2]{(\ref*{MC2})}} wherein the following identities are used:
			
			\smallskip
			\begin{itemize}
				\setlength{\itemsep}{7.9pt}
				\item[--\quad] $\operatorname{tr}(\bar\partial_{\operatorname{End} E}A(t)) = \bar\partial(\operatorname{tr} A(t))$;
				\item[--\quad] $\operatorname{tr}(\varphi(t)\lrcorner R_E) = \varphi(t)\lrcorner\operatorname{tr} R_E$;
				\item[--\quad]$\operatorname{tr}([A(t),A(t)]) = 0$;
				\item[--\quad] For the term $\operatorname{tr}\Big(\varphi(t)\lrcorner D_{\operatorname{End} E}^{1,0}A(t)\Big)$, we compute locally. In a local trivialisation, $$D_{\operatorname{End} E}^{1,0}A(t) = \partial A(t) + [\omega^{1,0},A(t)],$$ where $\omega^{1,0}$ is a matrix-valued $(1,0)$-form. Then this term equals
				\[
				\varphi(t)\lrcorner\operatorname{tr}\Big(D_{\operatorname{End} E}^{1,0}A(t)\Big) = \varphi(t)\lrcorner\Big(\operatorname{tr}(\partial A(t)) + \operatorname{tr}([\omega^{1,0},A(t)])\Big) = \varphi(t)\lrcorner\partial a(t).
				\]
			\end{itemize}
			
			\medskip
			Consequently, the trace-free part of \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[MC2]{(\ref*{MC2})}} becomes
			\begin{equation}\tag{TF}\label{tf}
				\bar\partial_{\operatorname{End} E} A^0(t) = \varphi(t) \lrcorner R_E^0 + \varphi(t) \lrcorner D_{\operatorname{End} E}^{1,0} A^0(t) - \frac{1}{2}[A(t),A(t)].
			\end{equation}
			
			Expanding in $t$, the $N$-th order obstruction equation for $N \ge 2$ takes the form
			\[
			\bar\partial A_N^0 = C_N^{\text{tf}},
			\]
			where $C_N^{\text{tf}}$ is $\bar\partial_{\operatorname{End} E}$-closed, \textit{provided that all obstructions up to order $N-1$ in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[tf]{(\ref*{tf})}} and all obstructions up to order $N$ in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[hhh]{(\ref*{hhh})}} vanish}.  Since $H^2(X,\operatorname{End}^0 E)=0$, we can solve for $A_N^0$ inductively. Hence
			\[
			A(t): = A^0(t) + \frac{a(t)}{r}\,\operatorname{id}_E
			\]
			satisfies \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[MC2]{(\ref*{MC2})}}. This completes the proof. 
		\end{proof}
		
		\begin{remark}
			The main differences between Proposition \ref{prop-1} and \cite[Proposition 4.10]{LRW19}, as well as \cite[Proposition I.3]{Zha26} (both with $D=\varnothing$), are two-fold:
			\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
				\item An additional obstruction equation (the third equation in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.2]{(\ref*{log 0.2})}}) needs to be solved simultaneously;
				\item The solutions $\varphi(t)$, $a(t)$ and $\Omega(t)$ are only required to be formal. 
				\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
					\item In the arguments of \cite{LRW19,Zha26}, the smoothness of the corresponding  $\Omega(t)$  was used to ensure that $\Omega(t)$ has no zeros for small $t$ (since $\Omega(0)$ is nowhere vanishing).  However, formal solutions suffice as shown above.
					\item   As for $\varphi(t)$ and $a(t)$, formal solutions are also enough: once they are obtained, we can then choose particularly nice solutions whose smoothness is very standard (see Proposition \ref{prop:formal-vs-canonical}). 
				\end{enumerate}
				This omits the regularity arguments  as in \cite[proof of Theorem 4.12, pp. 36-39]{LRW19} and \cite[Appendix I, Step (III)]{Zha26}.
			\end{enumerate}
		\end{remark}
		
		\begin{step}{Solve the obstruction equations: iteration}\label{step2}
		\end{step}
		
		By \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.2]{(\ref*{log 0.2})}}$_k$ we mean the part of \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.2]{(\ref*{log 0.2})}} formed by the first equation at order $k$ together with the second and third equations at order $k+1$. We now adopt an \textit{iterative} approach to solve \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.2]{(\ref*{log 0.2})}}.
		
		
		
		
		
		Before proceeding with the proof, we recall the following standard
		fact; see, for example, \cite[Proposition A.1]{HZ26} for a proof.
		
		\begin{lemma}\label{Fujiki}
			Let $X$ be a Fujiki manifold, and let $(F,h_F)$ be a Hermitian flat holomorphic
			vector bundle on $X$. Write its Chern connection as
			$
			\nabla_F=D_F^{1,0}+\bar\partial_F.
			$
			Then $(X,F)$ satisfies the
			$D_F^{1,0}\bar\partial_F$-lemma. More precisely, for every
			$\nabla_F$-closed $F$-valued $(p,q)$-form $\alpha$ on $X$, the
			following conditions are equivalent:
			\begin{equation*}
				\nabla_F\text{-exactness}
				\Longleftrightarrow
				D_F^{1,0}\text{-exactness}
				\Longleftrightarrow
				\bar\partial_F\text{-exactness}
				\Longleftrightarrow
				D_F^{1,0}\bar\partial_F\text{-exactness}.
			\end{equation*}
		\end{lemma}
		
		For $k=1$, the system \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.2]{(\ref*{log 0.2})}}$_1$ reads as
		\begin{equation}\label{123}
			\begin{dcases}
				\bar{\partial}_F\Omega_1 + D_F^{1,0} \bigl(\varphi_1 \lrcorner \Omega_0\bigr) = 0, \\[0.6em]
				\bar{\partial}_F\bigl(\varphi_2 \lrcorner \Omega_0 + \varphi_1 \lrcorner \Omega_1\bigr)
				+ \frac{1}{2}\, D_F^{1,0} \bigl(\varphi_1 \lrcorner (\varphi_1 \lrcorner \Omega_0)\bigr) = 0, \\[0.6em]
				\begin{aligned}
					\bar{\partial}a_2 \wedge \Omega_0 
					= &-\bar\partial a_1\wedge\Omega _1 + \bigl(\varphi_2 \lrcorner\operatorname{tr}  R_E \bigr) \wedge \Omega_0  +  \bigl(\varphi_1 \lrcorner \operatorname{tr} R_E \bigr) \wedge \Omega_1 +  \bigl(\varphi_1 \lrcorner \partial a_1 \bigr) \wedge \Omega_0. 
				\end{aligned}
			\end{dcases}
		\end{equation}
		From the first equation in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[123]{(\ref*{123})}}, we have
		\[
		\bar{\partial}_F D_F^{1,0}  (\varphi_1 \lrcorner \Omega_0)
		= - D_F^{1,0} \bar{\partial}_F (\varphi_1 \lrcorner \Omega_0)
		= - D_F^{1,0}  \bigl( (\bar{\partial} \varphi_1) \lrcorner \Omega_0 + \varphi_1 \lrcorner \bar{\partial}_F \Omega_0 \bigr) = 0,
		\]
		since $\bar{\partial}_F \Omega_0 = 0$ and $\bar{\partial} \varphi_1 = 0$. Hence, there exists 
		\begin{equation}\label{exact1}
			\textrm{a solution } \Omega_1
		\end{equation}
		thanks to Lemma \ref{Fujiki}.
		
		
		\medskip
		Likewise in the second equation of \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[123]{(\ref*{123})}}, since $D_F^{1,0}\bigl( \varphi_1 \lrcorner (\varphi_1 \lrcorner \Omega_0) \bigr)$ is $\bar{\partial}_F$-closed,  Lemma \ref{Fujiki} can be applied  again to $$\textrm{solve for } \varphi_2 \lrcorner \Omega_0,   \textrm{ and thus for } \varphi_2 \textrm{ itself,}$$ using the non-degeneracy of $\Omega_0$. Furthermore, one can ensure the existence of some $B_2\in A^{n-2,1}(X,F)$ such that 
		\begin{equation}\label{exact2}
			\varphi_2 \lrcorner \Omega_0 + \varphi_1 \lrcorner \Omega_1 = D_F^{1,0} B_2.
		\end{equation}
		
		
		\medskip
		For the third equation in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[123]{(\ref*{123})}}, its right-hand side is $\bar{\partial}_{ F}$-closed, since we have already solved for $\varphi_2$.
		For any $\theta \in A^{0,1}(X, T_X^{1,0})$ and bundle-valued forms $u, v$, we have \cite[p. 292]{Deme}
		\begin{equation}\label{contraction-formula}
			\theta \lrcorner (u \wedge v) = (\theta \lrcorner u) \wedge v + (-1)^{\deg u} u \wedge (\theta \lrcorner v).
		\end{equation}
		Therefore, by type reasons,
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:first}
			\bar{\partial} a_2 \wedge \Omega_0
			= -\bar\partial a_1 \wedge \Omega_1
			- \operatorname{tr} R_E \wedge (\varphi_2 \lrcorner \Omega_0 + \varphi_1 \lrcorner \Omega_1)
			- \partial a_1 \wedge (\varphi_1 \lrcorner \Omega_0).
		\end{equation}
		
		Using \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[exact2]{(\ref*{exact2})}}, \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[bianchi2]{(\ref*{bianchi2})}}, \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[exact1]{(\ref*{exact1})}}, and the Leibniz rule, we obtain
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:second}
			\begin{aligned}
				\bar{\partial}_F \bigl(a_2 \wedge \Omega_0\bigr)
				&= -\bar\partial a_1 \wedge \Omega_1
				- \operatorname{tr} R_E \wedge (D_F^{1,0} B_2)
				- \partial a_1 \wedge (\varphi_1 \lrcorner \Omega_0) \\[0.5em]
				&= -\bar\partial a_1 \wedge \Omega_1
				- D_F^{1,0}\bigl( \operatorname{tr} R_E \wedge B_2 - a_1 \wedge (\varphi_1 \lrcorner \Omega_0) \bigr)
				+ a_1 \wedge \bar\partial_F \Omega_1 \\[0.5em]
				&= -\bar\partial_F (a_1 \wedge \Omega_1)
				- D_F^{1,0}\bigl( \operatorname{tr} R_E \wedge B_2 - a_1 \wedge (\varphi_1 \lrcorner \Omega_0) \bigr).
			\end{aligned}
		\end{equation}
		Therefore, we can \begin{equation}\label{exact3}
			\textrm{solve for $a_2 \wedge \Omega_0 + a_1 \wedge \Omega_1$, and hence for $a_2$},
		\end{equation}  based on Lemma \ref{Fujiki}.
		
		
		
		\medskip
		\medskip
		\medskip
		By induction, assume that \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.2]{(\ref*{log 0.2})}}  is solvable for all $k \le N$, and that we have already found
		\[
		\Omega_i, \, 0 \le i \le N, \quad \varphi_i, \, 1 \le i \le N+1,  \quad \text{and} \quad a_i,  \, 1 \le i \le N+1.
		\]
		Thus, \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[hhh]{(\ref*{hhh})}} implies
		\begin{equation}\label{log 0.4}
			\bar{\partial} \varphi_k = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i+j=k} [\varphi_i, \varphi_j], \quad k \le N+1,
		\end{equation}
		and then 
		\begin{equation}\label{log 0.5}
			\bar{\partial} \Bigl( \sum_{i+j=k} [\varphi_i, \varphi_j] \Bigr) = 0, \quad k \le N+2,
		\end{equation}
		by using $[\alpha,\beta]=-[\beta,\alpha]$ for $\alpha\in A^{0,2} (X,T_X^{1,0})$ and arbitrary $\beta$.
		
		
		\medskip
		\medskip
		For the $(N+1)$-th step, \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.2]{(\ref*{log 0.2})}}$_{N+1}$ together with \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[contraction-formula]{(\ref*{contraction-formula})}} yields
		\begin{equation}\label{log 0.6}
			\begin{dcases}
				\bar{\partial}_F \Omega_{N+1} 
				+ \sum_{\substack{i+j=N+1}} D^{1,0}_{F}  \bigl({\varphi_i}\lrcorner \Omega_j \bigr) = 0, \\[0.8em]
				\sum_{\substack{i+j=N+2}} \bar{\partial}_F \bigl( {\varphi_i}\lrcorner \Omega_j \bigr)
				+ \sum_{\substack{i+j+k=N+2}} \frac{1}{2} D^{1,0}_{F}  \Bigl({\varphi_i}\lrcorner \bigl({\varphi_j}\lrcorner \Omega_k \bigr)\Bigr) = 0, \\[0.8em]
				\bar\partial_F \bigl(a_{N+2}\wedge\Omega_0\bigr)=-\sum_{\substack{i+j=N+2}}  \operatorname{tr} R_E\wedge\bigl(\varphi_i\lrcorner\Omega_j\bigr)-\sum_{\substack{i+j+k=N+2}} \partial a_i\wedge\bigl(\varphi_j\lrcorner\Omega_k\bigr)-\sum_{\substack{i+j=N+2,\,  j\geq 1}}\bar\partial a_i\wedge \Omega_j.
			\end{dcases}
		\end{equation}
		For the first equation  in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.6]{(\ref*{log 0.6})}}, 
		\allowdisplaybreaks
		\begin{align*}
			-\bar\partial_F \sum_{i+j=N+1} D^{1,0}_F(\varphi_i \lrcorner \Omega_j)
			&= D^{1,0}_F \Bigg(
			\sum_{i=1}^{N+1} \bar\partial \varphi_i \lrcorner \Omega_{N+1-i}
			+ \sum_{i=1}^{N+1} \varphi_i \lrcorner \bar\partial_F \Omega_{N+1-i}
			\Bigg) \\[0.9em]
			&= D^{1,0}_F \Bigg(
			\frac12 \sum_{i=1}^{N+1} \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} [\varphi_j,\varphi_{i-j}] \lrcorner \Omega_{N+1-i} \\
			&\qquad\qquad
			- \sum_{i=1}^{N+1} \varphi_i \lrcorner D^{1,0}_F \bigg(
			\sum_{j=1}^{N+1-i} \varphi_j \lrcorner \Omega_{N+1-i-j}
			\bigg)
			\Bigg) \\[0.9em]
			&= D^{1,0}_F \Bigg(
			\frac12 \sum_{i=1}^{N+1} \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \bigg(
			- D^{1,0}_F \bigl( \varphi_j \lrcorner (\varphi_{i-j} \lrcorner \Omega_{N+1-i}) \bigr) \\
			&\qquad\qquad\qquad
			+ \varphi_j \lrcorner D^{1,0}_F \bigl( \varphi_{i-j} \lrcorner \Omega_{N+1-i} \bigr)
			+ \varphi_{i-j} \lrcorner D^{1,0}_F \bigl( \varphi_j \lrcorner \Omega_{N+1-i} \bigr)
			\bigg) \\
			&\qquad
			- \sum_{i=1}^{N+1} \varphi_i \lrcorner D^{1,0}_F \bigg(
			\sum_{j=1}^{N+1-i} \varphi_j \lrcorner \Omega_{N+1-i-j}
			\bigg)
			\Bigg) \\[0.9em]
			&= D^{1,0}_F \Bigg(
			\sum_{1 \le j < i \le N+1} \varphi_j \lrcorner D^{1,0}_F \bigl( \varphi_{i-j} \lrcorner \Omega_{N+1-i} \bigr) \\
			&\qquad
			- \sum_{i=1}^{N+1} \varphi_i \lrcorner D^{1,0}_F \bigg(
			\sum_{j=1}^{N+1-i} \varphi_j \lrcorner \Omega_{N+1-i-j}
			\bigg)
			\Bigg) \\[0.6em]
			&= 0,
		\end{align*}
		where the third equality holds in view of   Lemma \ref{Tian-Todorov}.
		We then can   \begin{equation}\label{exact1'}
			\textrm{solve for } \Omega_{N+1}
		\end{equation}
		by Lemma \ref{Fujiki}.
		
		
		\medskip\medskip
		Moreover, for the second  equation  in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.6]{(\ref*{log 0.6})}}, 
		\begin{align*}
			&\quad \bar{\partial}_F \sum_{\substack{i+j+k=N+2}} D^{1,0}_{F}  \Bigl({\varphi_i}\lrcorner \bigl({\varphi_j}\lrcorner \Omega_k \bigr)\Bigr) \\
			&= \sum_{i+j+k=N+2} \bar{\partial}_F \Bigl(
			- [\varphi_j, \varphi_i] \lrcorner \Omega_k
			+ \varphi_i \lrcorner D^{1,0}_F \bigl(\varphi_j \lrcorner \Omega_k\bigr)
			+ \varphi_j \lrcorner D^{1,0}_F \bigl(\varphi_i \lrcorner \Omega_k\bigr)
			\Bigr) \\[0.6em]
			&= - \sum_{i+j+k=N+2} \bar{\partial}_F \bigl([\varphi_j, \varphi_i] \lrcorner \Omega_k\bigr)
			- 2 \sum_{\substack{j+k=N+2\\ k \ge 1}} \bar{\partial}_F \bigl(\varphi_j \lrcorner \bar{\partial}_F \Omega_k\bigr) \\[6pt]
			&= - \sum_{k=0}^{N+2} \Biggl( \bar{\partial} \sum_{i+j=N+2-k} [\varphi_j, \varphi_i] \Biggr) \lrcorner \Omega_k \\[3pt]
			&\quad + 2 \sum_{k=1}^{N+2} \Biggl( \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i+j=N+2-k} [\varphi_j, \varphi_i]
			- \bar{\partial} \varphi_{N+2-k} \Biggr) \lrcorner \bar{\partial}_F \Omega_k \\[6pt]
			&= 0,
		\end{align*}
		where the first equality is due to Lemma \ref{Tian-Todorov}, and the last equality uses \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.4]{(\ref*{log 0.4})}} and \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.5]{(\ref*{log 0.5})}}. Consequently, we can also $$\textrm{solve for $\sum_{\substack{i+j=N+2}} \varphi_i \lrcorner \Omega_j $,  and thus  for $\varphi_{N+2}$}.$$  Moreover,  we may ensure that
		\begin{equation}\label{exact 2'}
			\sum_{\substack{i+j=N+2}} \varphi_i \lrcorner \Omega_j = D_F^{1,0} B_{N+2}
		\end{equation}
		for some $B_{N+2}\in A^{n-2,1}(X,F)$ 	by Lemma \ref{Fujiki}.
		
		
		
		
		
		\medskip
		\medskip
		Finally, for the third equation in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.6]{(\ref*{log 0.6})}}, since we have already solved for $\varphi_k$ for $2\le k\le N+2$ and $a_k$ for $2\le k\le N+1$, its right-hand side is $\bar\partial_F$-closed. Moreover, using the solvability of \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.2]{(\ref*{log 0.2})}} for all $k\le N$, together with \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[exact 2']{(\ref*{exact 2'})}}, \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[bianchi2]{(\ref*{bianchi2})}}, \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[exact1']{(\ref*{exact1'})}}, and the Leibniz rule, we obtain
		\begin{equation}
			\begin{aligned}
				\bar{\partial}_F \bigl(a_{N+2}\wedge \Omega_0\bigr)
				&=-\sum_{\substack{i+j=N+2,\,  j\geq 1}}\bar\partial a_i\wedge \Omega_j
				- \operatorname{tr} R_E \wedge \bigl(D_F^{1,0} B_{N+2}\bigr)
				-\sum_{\substack{i+j+k=N+2}} \partial a_i\wedge\bigl(\varphi_j\lrcorner\Omega_k\bigr) \\[0.5em]
				&=-\sum_{\substack{i+j=N+2,\,  j\geq 1}}\bar\partial a_i\wedge \Omega_j
				- D_F^{1,0}\Biggl( \operatorname{tr} R_E \wedge B_{N+2} -  \sum_{\substack{i+j+k=N+2}}  a_i\wedge\bigl(\varphi_j\lrcorner\Omega_k\bigr)\Biggr)\\[0.2em]
				&\quad+ \sum_{\substack{i+j=N+2,\, j\geq 1}}a_i \wedge \bar\partial_F \Omega_j \\[0.5em]
				&= -\sum_{\substack{i+j=N+2,\, j\geq 1}} \bar\partial_F (a_i \wedge \Omega_j)
				- D_F^{1,0}\Biggl( \operatorname{tr} R_E \wedge B_{N+2} -  \sum_{\substack{i+j+k=N+2}}  a_i\wedge\bigl(\varphi_j\lrcorner\Omega_k\bigr)\Biggr).
			\end{aligned}
		\end{equation}
		Then Lemma \ref{Fujiki} applies to \begin{equation}\label{exact 3'}
			\textrm{solve for} \sum_{\substack{i+j=N+2}} a_i\wedge \Omega_j, \textrm{and hence for }  a_{N+2}.
		\end{equation}
		
		\medskip
		\medskip
		\medskip
		In summary, for given $\Omega_0, \varphi_1$ and $A_1$, we have constructed $\Omega_i$ for $1\le i\le N+1$, together with $\varphi_i$ and $a_i$ for $2\le i\le N+2$, such that \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.2]{(\ref*{log 0.2})}}$_{N+1}$ holds. Therefore,  the system \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.2]{(\ref*{log 0.2})}} admits a formal recursive solution. This completes the proof of Theorem \ref{main thm}.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-1}
			In the setting of Theorem  \ref{main thm},     for any first-order deformation 
			$\epsilon_1=(A_1,\varphi_1)$, suppose that there exist formal power series
			\[
			\varphi(t)=\sum_{i\geq 1}\varphi_i t^i \in A^{0,1}(X, T_X^{1,0})[[t]],\quad
			a(t)=\sum_{i\geq 1} a_i t^i  \in A^{0,1}(X,\mathcal O_X)[[t]], \quad a_1=\operatorname{tr} A_1,
			\]
			and
			\[
			\Omega(t)=\Omega_0+\sum_{i\geq 1}\Omega_i t^i\in A^{n,0}(X, F)[[t]],\quad	\Omega_0=\boldsymbol{\Omega},
			\]
			satisfying the system formally:
			\begin{equation}\tag{$\dagger$}\label{log 0.2}
				\begin{cases}
					\bigl(\bar\partial_F + D_F^{1,0}\circ \varphi(t)\lrcorner\bigr)\Omega(t)=0,\\[0.8em]
					\bigl(\bar\partial_F + \dfrac{1}{2}D_F^{1,0}\circ \varphi(t)\lrcorner\bigr)\bigl(\varphi(t)\lrcorner\Omega(t)\bigr)=0,\\[0.8em]
					\Bigl(		\bar\partial a(t)-\varphi(t) \lrcorner \operatorname{tr} R_E- \varphi(t)\lrcorner \partial a(t)\Bigr)\wedge\Omega(t)=0.\\
				\end{cases}
			\end{equation}
			Then the Kuranishi space of the pair $(X,E)$ is smooth.

label: aabb
title: Proof
body_md:
The first two 	equations in  \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.2]{(\ref*{log 0.2})}} together with Lemma \ref{Tian-Todorov} (noting that $\Omega(t)$ is automatically $D_F^{1,0}$-closed for type reasons) imply
			\begin{align*}
				\bar\partial\bigl(\varphi(t)\lrcorner \Omega(t)\bigr)
				&= -\frac{1}{2}\,D^{1,0}_F\Bigl(\varphi(t)\lrcorner\bigl(\varphi(t)\lrcorner\Omega(t)\bigr)\Bigr)\\
				&= \frac{1}{2}\,[\varphi(t),\varphi(t)]\lrcorner \Omega(t)
				- \varphi(t)\lrcorner D^{1,0}_F\bigl(\varphi(t)\lrcorner\Omega(t)\bigr)\\
				&= \frac{1}{2}\,[\varphi(t),\varphi(t)]\lrcorner \Omega(t)
				+ \varphi(t)\lrcorner\bar\partial\Omega(t).
			\end{align*}
			Hence
			\begin{equation}\label{aabb}
				\bigl(\bar\partial\varphi(t)\bigr)\lrcorner \Omega(t)
				= \bar\partial\bigl(\varphi(t)\lrcorner \Omega(t)\bigr)
				- \varphi(t)\lrcorner\bar\partial\Omega(t)
				= \frac{1}{2}\,[\varphi(t),\varphi(t)]\lrcorner \Omega(t).
			\end{equation}
			
			Set 
			\[
			V(t) := \bar\partial\varphi(t) - \frac{1}{2}[\varphi(t),\varphi(t)] = \sum_{i\ge 2} v_i t^i,
			\]
			with \(v_i \in A^{0,2}(X,T_X^{1,0})\). Then \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[aabb]{(\ref*{aabb})}} becomes \(V(t)\lrcorner\Omega(t)=0\).
			
			Locally write 
			\[
			\boldsymbol{\Omega} = f(z)\,dz^1\wedge\cdots\wedge dz^n\otimes e
			\]
			with \(f(z)\) nowhere vanishing and \(e\) a local frame of \(F\). Any \(v\in A^{0,2}(X,T_X^{1,0})\) can be expressed locally as
			\[
			v = \sum_{j=1}^n g_j\,\frac{\partial}{\partial z^j},
			\quad\text{where } g_j \text{ are smooth }(0,2)\text{-forms}.
			\]
			Contracting with \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) gives
			\[
			\boldsymbol{\Omega}\lrcorner v = f(z)\sum_{j=1}^n (-1)^{j-1} g_j\,
			dz^1\wedge\cdots\wedge\widehat{dz^j}\wedge\cdots\wedge dz^n\otimes e.
			\]
			The \((n-1,2)\)-forms appearing are linearly independent, hence the map \(v\mapsto\boldsymbol{\Omega}\lrcorner v\) is injective.
			
			
			\medskip
			Expanding
			\[
			V(t)\lrcorner\Omega(t)=\sum_{k\ge 2}\Bigl(\sum_{i+j=k}v_i\lrcorner\Omega_j\Bigr)t^k=0,
			\]
			we obtain:
			
			\begin{itemize}	\setlength{\itemsep}{5pt}
				\item[$\centerdot$] For \(k=2\), \(v_2\lrcorner\boldsymbol{\Omega}=0\), so \(v_2=0\) by injectivity.
				\item[$\centerdot$] Assume \(v_2=\dots=v_{N}=0\) for some \(N\ge 2\). Then the coefficient of \(t^{N+1}\) reduces to \(v_{N+1}\lrcorner\boldsymbol{\Omega}=0\), hence \(v_{N+1}=0\).
			\end{itemize}
			Therefore  \(V(t)=0\), i.e., 
			\begin{equation}\label{hhh}
				\bar\partial\varphi(t) = \dfrac{1}{2}[\varphi(t),\varphi(t)],
			\end{equation}
			namely the first obstruction equation \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[MC1]{(\ref*{MC1})}}.
			
			
			\medskip
			\medskip
			Via a similar argument, the third equation in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[log 0.2]{(\ref*{log 0.2})}} is equivalent to 
			\begin{equation}
				\bar\partial a(t)=\varphi(t) \lrcorner \operatorname{tr} R_E+ \varphi(t)\lrcorner \partial a(t).
			\end{equation}
			This is obtained by taking the trace of the second obstruction equation \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[MC2]{(\ref*{MC2})}} wherein the following identities are used:
			
			\smallskip
			\begin{itemize}
				\setlength{\itemsep}{7.9pt}
				\item[--\quad] $\operatorname{tr}(\bar\partial_{\operatorname{End} E}A(t)) = \bar\partial(\operatorname{tr} A(t))$;
				\item[--\quad] $\operatorname{tr}(\varphi(t)\lrcorner R_E) = \varphi(t)\lrcorner\operatorname{tr} R_E$;
				\item[--\quad]$\operatorname{tr}([A(t),A(t)]) = 0$;
				\item[--\quad] For the term $\operatorname{tr}\Big(\varphi(t)\lrcorner D_{\operatorname{End} E}^{1,0}A(t)\Big)$, we compute locally. In a local trivialisation, $$D_{\operatorname{End} E}^{1,0}A(t) = \partial A(t) + [\omega^{1,0},A(t)],$$ where $\omega^{1,0}$ is a matrix-valued $(1,0)$-form. Then this term equals
				\[
				\varphi(t)\lrcorner\operatorname{tr}\Big(D_{\operatorname{End} E}^{1,0}A(t)\Big) = \varphi(t)\lrcorner\Big(\operatorname{tr}(\partial A(t)) + \operatorname{tr}([\omega^{1,0},A(t)])\Big) = \varphi(t)\lrcorner\partial a(t).
				\]
			\end{itemize}
			
			\medskip
			Consequently, the trace-free part of \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[MC2]{(\ref*{MC2})}} becomes
			\begin{equation}\tag{TF}\label{tf}
				\bar\partial_{\operatorname{End} E} A^0(t) = \varphi(t) \lrcorner R_E^0 + \varphi(t) \lrcorner D_{\operatorname{End} E}^{1,0} A^0(t) - \frac{1}{2}[A(t),A(t)].
			\end{equation}
			
			Expanding in $t$, the $N$-th order obstruction equation for $N \ge 2$ takes the form
			\[
			\bar\partial A_N^0 = C_N^{\text{tf}},
			\]
			where $C_N^{\text{tf}}$ is $\bar\partial_{\operatorname{End} E}$-closed, \textit{provided that all obstructions up to order $N-1$ in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[tf]{(\ref*{tf})}} and all obstructions up to order $N$ in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[hhh]{(\ref*{hhh})}} vanish}.  Since $H^2(X,\operatorname{End}^0 E)=0$, we can solve for $A_N^0$ inductively. Hence
			\[
			A(t): = A^0(t) + \frac{a(t)}{r}\,\operatorname{id}_E
			\]
			satisfies \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[MC2]{(\ref*{MC2})}}. This completes the proof.

Therefore, we only need to verify the relevant weak $\partial\bar\partial$-lemmata of certain types. More precisely, by \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[exact1]{(\ref*{exact1})}} and \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[exact1']{(\ref*{exact1'})}} (resp.  \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[exact2]{(\ref*{exact2})}} and \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[exact 2']{(\ref*{exact 2'})}}; resp.  \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[exact3]{(\ref*{exact3})}} and \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[exact 3']{(\ref*{exact 3'})}}), this amounts to requiring that $X$ satisfies $\mathbb{S}^{n,1}$ (resp.  $\mathbb{B}^{n-1,2}$; resp. $\mathbb{S}^{n,2}$).

title: Proof
body_md:
Following the  beautiful strategy of Iacono--Manetti \cite{IM21}, we give an
		alternative proof of Theorem \ref{main thm}. The  \textit{only new}
		ingredient is Step \ref{step 1'}, where we  in particular prove the Fujiki case of the unobstructedness of
		locally trivial deformations of log pairs \((Y,\Delta)\) 
		with \(K_Y\otimes\mathcal{O}_Y(\Delta)\). Step \ref{step 2'} then applies the
		\(\mathbb P^1\)-bundle construction of Iacono--Manetti to deduce the
		unobstructedness of \((X,L)\), while Step \ref{step 3'} passes from
		\(L=\det E\) to \(E\). The last two steps are recalled from the cited
		references, and no originality is claimed for them.
		\setcounter{step}{0}
		
		\begin{step}{A $\bar\partial$-equation for twisted logarithmic forms: Fujiki version}\label{step 1'}
		\end{step}
		In this step, we extend the (weak) logarithmic
		$\partial\bar\partial$-lemma of \cite{Zha26}, together with its main
		applications, from compact K\"ahler manifolds to its \textit{bimeromorphic setting}.
		\begin{theorem}[{Fujiki version of \cite[Theorem  B]{Zha26}}]
			\label{dbar-Fujiki}
			Let $X$ be an $n$-dimensional Fujiki manifold, and let
			$D=\sum_{i=1}^sD_i$

		\end{tikzcd}
		\]

		\(

		\)
		the morphism $g$ is also bimeromorphic. Thus $Y$ is bimeromorphic to a compact K\"ahler manifold.

		$$
		Y=\mathbb{V}(L^*)\cup \Delta_\infty.

		\(
		\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb C}(\mathcal O_X,\mathcal O_X) \times \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(L,L)
		\)
		consisting of pairs $(h,u)$ satisfying
		\[
		u(ax)=h(a)x + a u(x)

	for all local sections $a$ of $\mathcal O_X$ and $x$ of $L$. 			Let $X$ be a compact complex manifold and $E$ a holomorphic vector bundle over $X$. Assume $H^2(X,\operatorname{End}^0 E)=0$, then the natural map
			\[
			\operatorname{Def}(X,E) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Def}(X,\det E)
			\]
			is smooth as a morphism of deformation functors.\footnote{
				Recall that a morphism $\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$
				of deformation functors is \textit{smooth} if, for every
				surjection $A'\twoheadrightarrow A$ of local Artin
				$\mathbb C$-algebras with residue field $\mathbb C$,
				the natural map
				$\mathcal F(A')\to
				\mathcal F(A)\times_{\mathcal G(A)}\mathcal G(A')$
				is surjective; see e.g.
				\cite[Definition  3.2.7]{Man22}.} In particular, if $(X,\det E)$ has unobstructed joint deformations, then so does $(X,E)$.
		\end{proposition}

				of deformation functors is \textit{smooth} if, for every
				surjection $A'\twoheadrightarrow A$ of local Artin
				$\mathbb C$-algebras with residue field $\mathbb C$,
				the natural map

				\mathcal F(A)\times_{\mathcal G(A)}\mathcal G(A')$

title: Proof
body_md:
Building on the sharp observation of Iacono--Manetti
		\cite[Remark 2.6]{IM21}, we show that their \(T^1\)-lifting argument
		also applies in our setting and provide further details for the
		reader's convenience.
		
		
		
		By Proposition \ref{reduction}, it suffices to consider the line bundle case. Set $L=\det E$.	Put the Artinian base \(A_m=\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^{m+1})\), and let
		\((X_m,L_m)\) be an arbitrary deformation of \((X,L)\) over \(A_m\).  Write
		\(\ell_m(\cdot)\) for the length of an \(A_m\)-module.
		
		By Deligne's Artinian length criterion \cite[(3.5.1)]{Del68},
		if \(C^\bullet\) is a bounded complex of finite free \(A_m\)-modules, then
		\begin{equation}\label{deligne}
			\ell_m H^i(C^\bullet)
			\leq
			(m+1)\dim_{\mathbb C}
			H^i(C^\bullet\otimes_{A_m}\mathbb C).
		\end{equation}
		Equality implies that \(H^i(C^\bullet)\) is free over \(A_m\) and compatible with reduction to $A_{m-1}$; namely, $$H^i(C^\bullet)\otimes_{A_m}A_{m-1}
		\xrightarrow{\simeq}
		H^i(C^\bullet\otimes_{A_m}A_{m-1}).$$
		
		Set
		\[
		H_m^{p,q}:=
		H^q(X_m,\Omega^p_{X_m/A_m}).
		\]
		The relative de Rham cohomology is topologically constant:
		\[
		H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(X_m/A_m)
		\simeq H^k(X,\mathbb C)\otimes_{\mathbb C}A_m.
		\]
		Consequently, applying \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[deligne]{(\ref*{deligne})}} to the Hodge--de Rham spectral sequence gives
		\begin{equation}\label{Degeneration}
			(m+1)b_k
			\leq
			\sum_{p+q=k}\ell_m H_m^{p,q}
			\leq
			(m+1)\sum_{p+q=k}h^{p,q}_{\bar\partial}(X).
		\end{equation}
		Since the \(\partial\bar\partial\)-lemma on $X_0$ implies degeneration at \(E_1\),
		\[
		b_k=\sum_{p+q=k}h^{p,q}_{\bar\partial}(X).
		\]
		Thus equality holds throughout \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[Degeneration]{(\ref*{Degeneration})}}.  Hence every \(H_m^{p,q}\) is free,
		satisfies base change and the relative Hodge--de Rham spectral
		sequence over  \(A_m\) degenerates at \(E_1\).
		
		In particular, a holomorphic volume form on \(X\) lifts to \(X_m\) and
		trivializes \(K_{X_m/A_m}\).  Contraction with this form gives
		\begin{equation}\label{iso}
			T^{1,0}_{X_m/A_m}\simeq\Omega^{n-1}_{X_m/A_m},
			\quad
			\mathcal O_{X_m}\simeq\Omega^n_{X_m/A_m}.
		\end{equation}
		
		
		
		Consider the relative Atiyah sequence
		\[
		0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{X_m}
		\longrightarrow A(L_m)
		\longrightarrow T^{1,0}_{X_m/A_m}
		\longrightarrow0.
		\]
		Its cohomology sequence contains
		\[
		H^0(T^{1,0}_{X_m/A_m})
		\xrightarrow{\alpha_{0,m}}H^1(\mathcal O_{X_m})
		\longrightarrow H^1(A(L_m))
		\longrightarrow H^1(T^{1,0}_{X_m/A_m})
		\xrightarrow{\alpha_{1,m}}H^2(\mathcal O_{X_m}),
		\]
		and therefore
		\begin{equation} \label{sequence}
			0\longrightarrow\operatorname{coker}\alpha_{0,m}
			\longrightarrow H^1(A(L_m))
			\longrightarrow\ker\alpha_{1,m}
			\longrightarrow0.
		\end{equation}
		
		
		Under \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[iso]{(\ref*{iso})}}, the two boundary maps are the Hodge components of cup product
		with \(c_1(L_m)\):
		\begin{equation}\label{chern}
			\alpha_{i,m}\colon
			H_m^{n-1,i}
			\xrightarrow{\;\cup c_1(L_m)\;}
			H_m^{n,i+1},
			\quad i=0,1.
		\end{equation}
		
		\medskip
		\textit{We now use the full strength of the \(\partial\bar\partial\)-lemma, rather than merely \(E_1\)-degeneration}. It identifies \(H_{\bar\partial}^{p,q}(X)\) with the subspace of \(H_{\mathrm{dR}}^{p+q}(X)\) represented by \(d\)-closed forms of pure type \((p,q)\), and gives the decomposition
		\[
		H_{\mathrm{dR}}^k(X,\mathbb C)
		=
		\bigoplus_{p+q=k}H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial}(X).
		\]
		
		\textit{In what follows,  we fix $k=n-1,n$.}     Consider the total cup-product maps
		\begin{equation*}
			T_0^k:
			H_{\mathrm{dR}}^k(X,\mathbb C)
			\longrightarrow
			H_{\mathrm{dR}}^{k+2}(X,\mathbb C)
		\end{equation*}
		and
		\begin{equation*}
			T_m^k:
			H_{\mathrm{dR}}^k(X_m/A_m)
			\longrightarrow
			H_{\mathrm{dR}}^{k+2}(X_m/A_m).
		\end{equation*}
		Since $k+2>n$, every nonzero Hodge component of
		$H_{\mathrm{dR}}^{k+2}(X,\mathbb C)$ has both bidegrees at least
		one. Consequently,
		\begin{equation*}
			H_{\mathrm{dR}}^{k+2}(X,\mathbb C)
			=
			\bigoplus_{p+q=k}
			H_{\bar\partial}^{p+1,q+1}(X),
		\end{equation*}
		and $T_0^k$ decomposes as the direct sum of the maps
		\begin{equation*}
			T_0^{p,q}:
			H_{\bar\partial}^{p,q}(X)
			\longrightarrow
			H_{\bar\partial}^{p+1,q+1}(X).
		\end{equation*}
		It follows that
		\begin{equation}\label{8}
			\dim_{\mathbb C}\ker T_0^k
			+
			\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{coker}T_0^k
			=
			\sum_{p+q=k}
			\left(
			\dim_{\mathbb C}\ker T_0^{p,q}
			+
			\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{coker}T_0^{p,q}
			\right).
		\end{equation}
		
		Under the topological identification of relative de Rham cohomology, \(c_1(L_m)\) corresponds to \(c_1(L)\otimes1\), hence
		\begin{equation}\label{9}
			T_m^k=T_0^k\otimes_{\mathbb C}A_m. 
		\end{equation}
		Moreover, $T_m^k$ raises the relative Hodge filtration by one, and its associated-graded maps  are
		\[
		T_m^{p,q}\colon
		H_m^{p,q}\longrightarrow H_m^{p+1,q+1},
		\quad p+q=k.
		\]
		These include the boundary maps in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[chern]{(\ref*{chern})}}:
		\[
		\alpha_{i,m}=T_m^{n-1,i},
		\quad i=0,1.
		\]
		
		Applying the spectral-sequence length inequality to the filtered two-term complex defined by \(T_m^k\), and Deligne's inequality \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[deligne]{(\ref*{deligne})}} to the two-term complexes defined by \(T_m^{p,q}\), gives
		\begin{equation*}\label{length-chain}
			\begin{aligned}
				(m+1)\Bigl(
				\dim_{\mathbb C}\ker T_0^k
				+\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{coker}T_0^k
				\Bigr)
				&=
				\ell_m\bigl(\ker T_m^k\bigr)
				+\ell_m\bigl(\operatorname{coker}T_m^k\bigr)\\[0.5em]
				&\le
				\sum_{p+q=k}\Bigl(
				\ell_m\bigl(\ker T_m^{p,q}\bigr)
				+\ell_m\bigl(\operatorname{coker}T_m^{p,q}\bigr)
				\Bigr)\\[0.5em]
				&\le
				(m+1)\sum_{p+q=k}\Bigl(
				\dim_{\mathbb C}\ker T_0^{p,q}
				+\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{coker}T_0^{p,q}
				\Bigr)\\[0.5em]
				&=
				(m+1)\Bigl(
				\dim_{\mathbb C}\ker T_0^k
				+\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{coker}T_0^k
				\Bigr).
			\end{aligned}
		\end{equation*}
		where the first equality follows from \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[9]{(\ref*{9})}}, and the last from \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[8]{(\ref*{8})}}. Hence equality holds throughout.
		
		As a result, 
		\[
		\operatorname{coker}\alpha_{0,m}
		=
		\operatorname{coker}T_m^{n-1,0},
		\quad
		\ker\alpha_{1,m}
		=
		\ker T_m^{n-1,1}
		\]
		are free and compatible with  base change. 
		It now follows from \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[sequence]{(\ref*{sequence})}} that \(H^1(A(L_m))\) is free over \(A_m\) and that
		\[
		H^1(A(L_m))\otimes_{A_m}A_{m-1}
		\simeq
		H^1(A(L_{m-1})).
		\]
		In particular,
		\[
		H^1(A(L_m))
		\longrightarrow
		H^1(A(L_{m-1}))
		\]
		is surjective. This is precisely the  \textit{\(T^1\)-lifting property} for the pair \((X,L)\)  and hence it  has  unobstructed deformations.

label: wells
title: Proof
body_md:
We first   record a useful consequence due to Wells. 
		\begin{lemma}[{\cite[Theorem 3.1 (c)]{Wel74}}]\label{wells}
			Let $f: Y \to X$ be a proper surjective morphism between two equidimensional complex manifolds, and let $E$ be a holomorphic vector bundle over $X$. Then $f$ induces injections for all $p$ and $q$:
			\[
			f^*: H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial}(X, E) \lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial}(Y, f^*E).
			\]
		\end{lemma}
		If $X$ is a Fujiki manifold then it is a
		$\partial\bar\partial$-manifold. By the above $T^1$-lifting proof, it suffices to
		consider the case in which $K_X$ is torsion. Then there exists a finite
		\'etale cover
		\(\pi:\widetilde{X}\to X\) such that
		\(K_{\widetilde{X}} \simeq \mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}}\)
		(see, e.g., \cite{Par91}). 
		Let \(f:Y\to X\) be a proper modification from a compact K\"ahler
		manifold \(Y\), and set
		\(\widetilde{Y}:=Y\times_X\widetilde{X}\).
		We then obtain the commutative diagram
		\begin{equation}\label{diagram}
			\begin{tikzcd}
				\widetilde{Y}
				\arrow[d, "\widetilde{\pi}"']
				\arrow[r, "\widetilde{f}"]
				& \widetilde{X} \arrow[d, "\pi"] \\
				Y \arrow[r, "f"] & X.
			\end{tikzcd}
		\end{equation}
		By stability under base change, \(\widetilde{\pi}\) remains finite
		\'etale, while \(\widetilde{f}\) is bimeromorphic.
		In particular, \(\widetilde{Y}\) is again a compact K\"ahler manifold, therefore \(\widetilde{X}\) is also a Fujiki manifold.
		
		
		Now for any \(N\geq 1\), let
		\[
		v_N := \frac{1}{2}\left\{\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}(A_i,\varphi_i),
		(A_{N+1-i},\varphi_{N+1-i})\right]\right\}
		\;\in\; H^2\bigl(X,A(L)\bigr), \,\,\text{with }L=\det E,
		\]
		be an \(N\)-th order obstruction class.
		Since \(\pi\) is \'etale, it is proper and surjective, Lemma \ref{wells} implies that
		the pull-back map
		\[
		\pi^* \colon H^2\bigl(X,A(L)\bigr)
		\longrightarrow
		H^2\bigl(\widetilde{X},A(\pi^*L)\bigr)
		\]
		is injective, which completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $K_X\simeq\mathcal O_X$ and
		$(\operatorname{End}^0E)^\vee\simeq\operatorname{End}^0E$,
		Serre duality gives
		$$
		H^2(X,\operatorname{End}^0E)
		\simeq
		H^0(X,\operatorname{End}^0E)^\vee
		=0,
		$$
		where the last equality follows from the simplicity of $E$.
		To apply Theorem \ref{main thm2}, it remains to verify the three weak $\partial\bar\partial$-conditions. For this, we use the following observation. 
		\begin{proposition}\label{prop:weak-surface}
			Let \(X\) be a compact complex surface. Then \(X\) always
			satisfies \(\mathbb S^{2,2}\) and \(\mathbb B^{1,2}\).
			Moreover, \(X\) satisfies \(\mathbb S^{2,1}\)
			if and only  \(X\) is K\"ahler.
		\end{proposition}
		
		\begin{proof}
			We first recall the cohomological characterization of the weak
			conditions. The Bott--Chern and Aeppli cohomology groups are
			defined by
			\begin{equation*}
				H_{\mathrm{BC}}^{p,q}(X)
				:=
				\frac{
					\ker\partial\cap\ker\bar\partial
				}{
					\operatorname{im}\partial\bar\partial
				},
				\qquad
				H_{\mathrm A}^{p,q}(X)
				:=
				\frac{
					\ker\partial\bar\partial
				}{
					\operatorname{im}\partial+\operatorname{im}\bar\partial
				}.
			\end{equation*}
			By \cite[p.  3009]{RZ18}, the condition
			\(\mathbb S^{p,q}\) is equivalent to the injectivity of
			\begin{equation}\label{eq:characterization-S}
				\iota_{\bar\partial,\mathrm A}^{p,q}:
				H_{\bar\partial}^{p,q}(X)
				\longrightarrow
				H_{\mathrm A}^{p,q}(X),
			\end{equation}
			whereas \(\mathbb B^{p,q}\) is equivalent to the injectivity of
			\begin{equation}\label{eq:characterization-B}
				\iota_{\mathrm{BC},\partial}^{p,q}:
				H_{\mathrm{BC}}^{p,q}(X)
				\longrightarrow
				H_{\partial}^{p,q}(X).
			\end{equation}
			
			
			We first verify \(\mathbb S^{2,2}\). Let
			\(\partial g\in A^{2,2}(X)\). Since
			\(\bar\partial g=0\) for dimensional reasons, Stokes' theorem
			gives
			\begin{equation*}
				\int_X\partial g=\int_Xdg=0.
			\end{equation*}
			By Serre duality, integration identifies
			\(H_{\bar\partial}^{2,2}(X)\) with \(\mathbb C\). Hence
			\([\partial g]_{\bar\partial}=0\), proving
			\(\mathbb S^{2,2}\).
			
			Second, $\mathbb B^{1,2}$ always holds. Indeed, by \cite[Theorem  1.1 (i)]{ADT16}, the natural map\begin{equation*}H_{\mathrm{BC}}^{2,1}(X)\longrightarrow H_{\bar\partial}^{2,1}(X)\end{equation*}is injective for every compact complex surface. Taking complex conjugates then gives the injectivity of $H_{\mathrm{BC}}^{1,2}(X)\longrightarrow H_{\partial}^{1,2}(X)$ and hence $X$ satisfies $\mathbb B^{1,2}$.
			
			It remains to characterize the condition $\mathbb S^{2,1}$.
			Suppose that $X$ satisfies $\mathbb S^{2,1}$. By
			\textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[eq:characterization-S]{(\ref*{eq:characterization-S})}} and duality, the natural map
			\begin{equation*}
				H_{\mathrm{BC}}^{0,1}(X)
				\longrightarrow
				H_{\bar\partial}^{0,1}(X)
			\end{equation*}
			is surjective. This map is always injective. Indeed, if
			$\alpha=\bar\partial f$ represents a Bott--Chern class, then
			$\partial\alpha=0$ gives $\partial\bar\partial f=0$. Since every
			global pluriharmonic function on a compact complex manifold is
			constant, we have $\alpha=0$. Consequently,
			\begin{equation}\label{eq:BC01-bar01}
				h_{\mathrm{BC}}^{0,1}(X)
				=
				h_{\bar\partial}^{0,1}(X).
			\end{equation}
			
			On the other hand, the Fr\"olicher spectral sequence of every compact
			complex surface degenerates at $E_1$
			\cite[Theorem  IV.2.8]{BHPV04}. In particular, every holomorphic
			one-form is $d$-closed, and hence
			\begin{equation}\label{eq:BC10-bar10}
				h_{\mathrm{BC}}^{1,0}(X)
				=
				h_{\bar\partial}^{1,0}(X).
			\end{equation}
			Complex conjugation for Bott--Chern cohomology gives
			$
			h_{\mathrm{BC}}^{1,0}(X)
			=
			h_{\mathrm{BC}}^{0,1}(X).
			$
			Combining this equality with
			\textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[eq:BC01-bar01]{(\ref*{eq:BC01-bar01})}} and \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[eq:BC10-bar10]{(\ref*{eq:BC10-bar10})}}, we obtain
			\begin{equation*}
				h_{\bar\partial}^{1,0}(X)
				=
				h_{\bar\partial}^{0,1}(X).
			\end{equation*}
			
			The $E_1$-degeneration also gives
			\begin{equation*}
				b_1(X)
				=
				h_{\bar\partial}^{1,0}(X)
				+
				h_{\bar\partial}^{0,1}(X)
				=
				2h_{\bar\partial}^{0,1}(X).
			\end{equation*}
			Thus $b_1(X)$ is even, and therefore $X$ is K\"ahler by
			\cite[Theorem  11]{Buchdahl} or 	\cite[Theorem  IV.3.1]{BHPV04}.
			
			Conversely, if $X$ is K\"ahler, then it satisfies the
			$\partial\bar\partial$-lemma and hence $\mathbb S^{2,1}$.
		\end{proof}
		The proof of Corollary \ref{simple} is therefore completed.

			\textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[eq:BC01-bar01]{(\ref*{eq:BC01-bar01})}} and \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[eq:BC10-bar10]{(\ref*{eq:BC10-bar10})}}, we obtain
			\begin{equation*}
				h_{\bar\partial}^{1,0}(X)
				=
				h_{\bar\partial}^{0,1}(X).
			\end{equation*}
			
			The $E_1$-degeneration also gives
			\begin{equation*}
				b_1(X)
				=
				h_{\bar\partial}^{1,0}(X)
				+
				h_{\bar\partial}^{0,1}(X)
				=
				2h_{\bar\partial}^{0,1}(X).
			\end{equation*}
			Thus $b_1(X)$ is even, and therefore $X$ is K\"ahler by
			\cite[Theorem  11]{Buchdahl} or 	\cite[Theorem  IV.3.1]{BHPV04}.
			
			Conversely, if $X$ is K\"ahler, then it satisfies the
			$\partial\bar\partial$-lemma and hence $\mathbb S^{2,1}$.

body_md:
Consider the connected complex Lie group
		\[
		G=\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb C).
		\]
		By examples due to Ghys \cite{Ghy95} and Winkelmann \cite{Win95},
		recalled in \cite[Introduction]{KS23}, one may choose a cocompact
		lattice $\Gamma\subset G$ such that
		\[
		X:=\Gamma\backslash G
		\]
		is a page-$1$-$\partial\bar\partial$-manifold; see
		\cite[Definition  2.10]{PSU24} for the terminology.
		
		Choose a basis of left-invariant holomorphic one-forms
		$\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3$ on $X$ satisfying
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:sl2-structure}
			\partial\omega_1
			=
			\omega_2\wedge\omega_3,
			\qquad
			\partial\omega_2
			=
			\omega_3\wedge\omega_1,
			\qquad
			\partial\omega_3
			=
			\omega_1\wedge\omega_2.
		\end{equation}
		
		\begin{enumerate}[{(1)}]
			\item
			\textit{First, $X$ is $K$-trivial Calabi--Yau.}
			Indeed, the form
			\begin{equation*}
				\Omega_X
				:=
				\omega_1\wedge\omega_2\wedge\omega_3
			\end{equation*}
			is nowhere vanishing. Hence $K_X\simeq\mathcal O_X$.
			
			\medskip
			\item
			\textit{We next verify the three weak
				$\partial\bar\partial$-conditions.}
			Put
			\begin{equation*}
				\mathrm P_X^\bullet
				:=
				\Lambda^\bullet
				\langle\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3\rangle
			\end{equation*}
			and consider the double complex of left-invariant forms
			\begin{equation*}
				\mathcal I_X^{p,q}
				:=
				\mathrm P_X^p
				\otimes
				\overline{\mathrm P_X^q}.
			\end{equation*}
			By Akhiezer's theorem \cite{Akh97} and the proof of
			\cite[Corollary  13]{KS23}, the inclusion
			$	\mathcal I_X^{\bullet,\bullet}
			\hookrightarrow
			A^{\bullet,\bullet}(X)
			$
			induces isomorphisms in Dolbeault cohomology. (We remark that the choice of $\Gamma$ is essential here: for an arbitrary lattice,
			left-invariant forms need not compute the Dolbeault cohomology.)  By complex
			conjugation, it also induces isomorphisms in
			$\partial$-cohomology.   \cite[Corollary  5]{KS23} then
			implies that the same inclusion induces isomorphisms in
			Bott--Chern and Aeppli cohomology. Therefore the natural maps
			used to verify $\mathbb S^{p,q}$ and $\mathbb B^{p,q}$ may
			be computed on $\mathcal I_X^{\bullet,\bullet}$.
			
			The structure equations show that
			\begin{equation*}
				\partial:
				\mathrm P_X^1
				\longrightarrow
				\mathrm P_X^2
			\end{equation*}
			is an isomorphism and that $\partial\mathrm P_X^2=0$. Indeed,
			\begin{equation*}
				\partial\mathrm P_X^1
				=
				\left\langle
				\omega_2\wedge\omega_3,\,
				\omega_3\wedge\omega_1,\,
				\omega_1\wedge\omega_2
				\right\rangle
				=
				\mathrm P_X^2,
			\end{equation*}
			while \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[eq:sl2-structure]{(\ref*{eq:sl2-structure})}} directly gives
			$\partial\mathrm P_X^2=0$. Consequently,
			\begin{equation}\label{eq:sl2-small-cohomology}
				H^1(\mathrm P_X^\bullet,\partial)=0,
				\quad
				H^2(\mathrm P_X^\bullet,\partial)=0,
				\quad
				H^3(\mathrm P_X^\bullet,\partial)
				=
				\mathbb C[\Omega_X].
			\end{equation}
			
			It follows from \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[eq:sl2-small-cohomology]{(\ref*{eq:sl2-small-cohomology})}} and complex
			conjugation that
			\begin{equation*}
				H_{\bar\partial}^{3,1}(X)=0,
				\quad
				H_{\bar\partial}^{3,2}(X)=0.
			\end{equation*}
			Thus
			$\iota_{\bar\partial,\mathrm A}^{3,1}$ and
			$\iota_{\bar\partial,\mathrm A}^{3,2}$ are injective, and
			hence $Y$ satisfies $\mathbb S^{3,1}$ and
			$\mathbb S^{3,2}$.
			
			It remains to check $\mathbb B^{2,2}$. Since
			$\partial\mathrm P_X^2=0$ and
			$\bar\partial\overline{\mathrm P_X^2}=0$, every element of
			$\mathrm P_X^2\otimes\overline{\mathrm P_X^2}$ is both
			$\partial$-closed and $\bar\partial$-closed. Moreover,
			\begin{equation*}
				\partial\mathrm P_X^1=\mathrm P_X^2,
				\quad
				\bar\partial\overline{\mathrm P_X^1}
				=
				\overline{\mathrm P_X^2}.
			\end{equation*}
			We therefore obtain
			\begin{align*}
				H_{\mathrm{BC}}^{2,2}(X)
				\simeq
				H_{\mathrm{BC}}^{2,2}(\mathcal I_X)=
				\frac{
					\mathrm P_X^2
					\otimes
					\overline{\mathrm P_X^2}
				}{
					\partial\mathrm P_X^1
					\otimes
					\bar\partial\overline{\mathrm P_X^1}
				}
				=0.
			\end{align*}
			Hence $\iota_{\mathrm{BC},\partial}^{2,2}$ is injective,
			and $Y$ satisfies
			$
			\mathbb B^{2,2}.$
			
			
			We shall also need two further injectivities in the next
			example. Since $\partial\mathrm P_X^2=0$, for every $q$ the
			map
			\begin{equation*}
				\iota_{\mathrm{BC},\partial}^{3,q}:
				H_{\mathrm{BC}}^{3,q}(X)
				\longrightarrow
				H_{\partial}^{3,q}(X)
			\end{equation*}
			is identified with the inclusion
			\begin{equation*}
				\mathrm P_X^3
				\otimes
				\ker\left(
				\bar\partial:
				\overline{\mathrm P_X^q}
				\longrightarrow
				\overline{\mathrm P_X^{q+1}}
				\right)
				\hookrightarrow
				\mathrm P_X^3
				\otimes
				\overline{\mathrm P_X^q}.
			\end{equation*}
			In particular, $X$ also satisfies
			$
			\mathbb B^{3,0}
			$ and $
			\mathbb B^{3,1}.
			$
			
			
					\medskip
			\item
			\textit{We now show that \(
				E_1^{\bullet,\bullet}(X)
				\not\simeq
				E_\infty^{\bullet,\bullet}(X)
				\).}
			Notice that
			\begin{equation*}
				\bar\partial\omega_1=0,
				\qquad
				d_1[\omega_1]
				=
				[\partial\omega_1]
				=
				[\omega_2\wedge\omega_3]
				\neq0.
			\end{equation*}
			The last class is nonzero because a nonzero form of type
			$(2,0)$ cannot be $\bar\partial$-exact. Thus the Fr\"olicher
			spectral sequence of $X$ does not degenerate at $E_1$.
			
					\medskip
			\item
			\textit{We finally verify \ref{4444}.}  By
			\textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[eq:sl2-small-cohomology]{(\ref*{eq:sl2-small-cohomology})}} and complex conjugation, 
			$H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)=0. $  Therefore
			$H^2(X,T_X^{1,0})=0$
			since $X$ is complex parallelisable. 
			Let $E\rightarrow X$ be a holomorphic vector bundle satisfying
			$H^2(X,\operatorname{End}^{0}E)=0$. By \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[direct sum]{(\ref*{direct sum})}}, 
			$H^2(X,\operatorname{End}E)=0.$
			The Atiyah sequence
			\begin{equation*}
				0\longrightarrow
				\operatorname{End}E
				\longrightarrow
				A(E)
				\longrightarrow
				T_X^{1,0}
				\longrightarrow0
			\end{equation*}
			then gives
			\begin{equation*}
				H^2(X,A(E))=0.
			\end{equation*}
		\end{enumerate}

body_md:
Let
		\begin{equation*}
			\zeta:=e^{\pi i/3},
			\quad
			R:=\mathbb Z[\zeta],
			\quad
			B:=\mathbb C/R.
		\end{equation*}
		Consider the complex Heisenberg group $H=\mathbb C^3$, with
		multiplication
		\begin{equation*}
			(z_1,z_2,z_3)(w_1,w_2,w_3)
			=
			(z_1+w_1,z_2+w_2,z_3+w_3+z_1w_2),
		\end{equation*}
		and its cocompact lattice $\Gamma:=R^3$.
		Set $N:=\Gamma\backslash H$.
		The automorphism
		\begin{equation*}
			\phi(z_1,z_2,z_3)
			=
			(\zeta z_1,\zeta z_2,\zeta^2z_3)
		\end{equation*}
		preserves $\Gamma$ and therefore descends to $N$.
		
		
				\medskip
		On $\widetilde X:=N\times B^3$, define
		\begin{equation*}
			g(z,x,y,t)
			=
			\left(\phi(z),\zeta^2x,y+\frac16,t\right).
		\end{equation*}
		This generates a free action of a cyclic group of order $6$:
		for $1\leq k\leq5$, the map $g^k$ translates the
		$y$-coordinate by the nonzero element $\frac k6$ of $B$.
		Thus
		\begin{equation*}
			X:=\widetilde X/\langle g\rangle
		\end{equation*}
		is a compact complex sixfold.
		Since $g$ acts trivially on the last factor,
		$X=Z\times B$, where $Z$ is the quotient of $N\times B^2$
		by the induced action. Denote the projection to the last
		factor by $$f:X\longrightarrow B.$$
		
		On $\widetilde X$, consider the holomorphic coframe
		\begin{equation*}
			\alpha_1=dz_1,\quad
			\alpha_2=dz_2,\quad
			\alpha_3=dz_3-z_1dz_2,\quad
			\alpha_4=dx,\quad
			\alpha_5=dy,\quad
			\alpha_6=dt.
		\end{equation*}
		Writing
		$\alpha_{j_1\cdots j_k}
		:=\alpha_{j_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_{j_k}$,
		we have
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:nilpotent-structure}
			\partial\alpha_3=-\alpha_{12},
			\quad
			\partial\alpha_j=0
			\quad(j\neq3),
		\end{equation}
		and
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:cyclic-action}
			g^*(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_6)
			=
			(\zeta\alpha_1,\zeta\alpha_2,
			\zeta^2\alpha_3,\zeta^2\alpha_4,
			\alpha_5,\alpha_6).
		\end{equation}
		We identify $g$-invariant forms on $\widetilde X$ with
		their descended forms on $X$.
		
		\begin{enumerate}[{(1)}]
			\item
			\textit{First, $K_X$ is trivial.}
			The nowhere-vanishing holomorphic form
			\begin{equation*}
				\Omega:=\alpha_{123456}
			\end{equation*}
			is $g$-invariant, since $\zeta^{1+1+2+2}=1$.
			It therefore descends to $X$, proving
			$K_X\simeq\mathcal O_X$.
			
			
					\medskip
			\item
			\textit{We next verify the three weak
				$\partial\bar\partial$-conditions.}
			Put
			\begin{equation*}
				\mathrm P^\bullet
				:=
				\Lambda^\bullet
				\langle\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_6\rangle,
				\quad
				\mathcal I^{p,q}
				:=
				\left(
				\mathrm P^p\otimes\overline{\mathrm P^q}
				\right)^{\langle g\rangle}.
			\end{equation*}
			By Sakane's theorem \cite[Theorem  1]{Sak76},
			left-invariant forms compute the Dolbeault cohomology
			of $\widetilde X$. Since taking invariants under a
			finite group is exact, the inclusion
			\begin{equation*}
				\mathcal I^{\bullet,\bullet}
				\hookrightarrow
				A^{\bullet,\bullet}(X)
			\end{equation*}
			also induces isomorphisms in Dolbeault cohomology.
			By complex conjugation and \cite[Corollary  5]{KS23},
			it induces isomorphisms in $\partial$-, Bott--Chern
			and Aeppli cohomology as well.
			Thus the natural maps characterizing the weak
			conditions may be computed on
			$\mathcal I^{\bullet,\bullet}$.
			
					\medskip
			By \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[eq:cyclic-action]{(\ref*{eq:cyclic-action})}},
			\begin{equation*}
				\begin{aligned}
					\mathcal I^{6,1}
					&=
					\left\langle
					\Omega\wedge\bar\alpha_5,\,
					\Omega\wedge\bar\alpha_6
					\right\rangle,
					\\
					\mathcal I^{6,2}
					&=
					\mathbb C\,
					\Omega\wedge\bar\alpha_{56}.
				\end{aligned}
			\end{equation*}
			These forms are $\bar\partial$-closed. Moreover,
			\begin{equation*}
				\partial\mathrm P^5=0,
				\quad
				\bar\partial\mathcal I^{6,0}
				=
				\bar\partial\mathcal I^{6,1}
				=
				0.
			\end{equation*}
			Consequently, for $q=1,2$, both
			$H_{\bar\partial}^{6,q}(X)$ and
			$H_{\mathrm A}^{6,q}(X)$ are identified with
			$\mathcal I^{6,q}$, and the natural map between them
			is the identity. Hence $X$ satisfies
			$\mathbb S^{6,1}$ and $\mathbb S^{6,2}$.
			
					\medskip
			It remains to check $\mathbb B^{5,2}$.
			The same action gives
			\begin{equation*}
				\begin{aligned}
					\mathcal I^{5,2}
					=
					\bigl\langle\,
					&
					\alpha_{12345}\wedge\bar\alpha_{56},\,
					\alpha_{12346}\wedge\bar\alpha_{56},
					\\
					&
					\alpha_{12356}\wedge\bar\alpha_{34},\,
					\alpha_{12456}\wedge\bar\alpha_{34}
					\,\bigr\rangle.
				\end{aligned}
			\end{equation*}
			All four generators are $\partial$-closed, while
			the $\bar\partial$-closed subspace is spanned by
			the first two, since
			$\bar\partial\bar\alpha_{34}=-\bar\alpha_{124}$.
			Furthermore,
			\begin{equation*}
				\partial\mathcal I^{4,2}
				=
				\mathbb C\,
				\alpha_{12456}\wedge\bar\alpha_{34},
			\end{equation*}
			which contains no nonzero $\bar\partial$-closed
			element. Thus, in the invariant double complex
			$\mathcal I^{\bullet,\bullet}$, there are no nonzero
			$\partial\bar\partial$-boundaries in bidegree $(5,2)$.
			We obtain
			\begin{equation*}
				\begin{aligned}
					H_{\mathrm{BC}}^{5,2}(X)
					&=
					\left\langle
					[\alpha_{12345}\wedge\bar\alpha_{56}],
					[\alpha_{12346}\wedge\bar\alpha_{56}]
					\right\rangle,
					\\
					H_\partial^{5,2}(X)
					&=
					\left\langle
					[\alpha_{12345}\wedge\bar\alpha_{56}],
					[\alpha_{12346}\wedge\bar\alpha_{56}],
					[\alpha_{12356}\wedge\bar\alpha_{34}]
					\right\rangle.
				\end{aligned}
			\end{equation*}
			The natural map is the inclusion of the first two
			classes. Therefore $X$ satisfies $\mathbb B^{5,2}$.
			
			
					\medskip
			\item
			\textit{We now show that the Fr\"olicher spectral
				sequence does not degenerate at $E_1$.}
			The form $\alpha_3\wedge\bar\alpha_4$ is
			$g$-invariant and $\bar\partial$-closed, and
			\begin{equation*}
				d_1[\alpha_3\wedge\bar\alpha_4]
				=
				-[\alpha_{12}\wedge\bar\alpha_4]
				\neq0.
			\end{equation*}
			Indeed, the last class is already nonzero on
			$\widetilde X$, whose Dolbeault cohomology in this
			bidegree is
			$\mathrm P^2\otimes
			H^1(\overline{\mathrm P^\bullet},\bar\partial)$,
			and $[\bar\alpha_4]\neq0$.
			In particular, $X$ does not satisfy the full
			$\partial\bar\partial$-lemma.
			
			
					\medskip
			\item
			\textit{Finally, we construct $E$ and compute its
				obstruction space.}
			Recall that a holomorphic vector bundle $V$ over $B$
			is \textit{stable} if
			$\frac{\deg S}{\operatorname{rank}S}
			<
			\frac{\deg V}{\operatorname{rank}V}$
			for every nonzero proper holomorphic subbundle
			$S\subset V$.
			
			Let $o:=[0]\in B$ be the origin and choose a nonsplit
			extension
			\begin{equation*}
				0
				\longrightarrow
				\mathcal O_B
				\longrightarrow
				F
				\longrightarrow
				\mathcal O_B(o)
				\longrightarrow
				0.
			\end{equation*}
			Such an extension exists since
			$H^1(B,\mathcal O_B(-o))\simeq\mathbb C$.
			Then $F$ has rank $2$ and degree $1$.
			If a line subbundle $S\subset F$ had $\deg S\geq1$,
			the composite $S\to F\to\mathcal O_B(o)$ would be
			nonzero, since
			$\operatorname{Hom}(S,\mathcal O_B)=0$.
			As $\deg\mathcal O_B(o)=1$, this composite would be
			an isomorphism, splitting the extension.
			Thus every line subbundle has degree at most $0$,
			so $F$ is stable and hence simple by
			\cite[Chapter  V, Corollary  7.14]{Kob87}.
			Since $K_B\simeq\mathcal O_B$, Serre duality gives
			\begin{equation*}
				H^0(B,\operatorname{End}^{0}F)
				=
				H^1(B,\operatorname{End}^{0}F)
				=
				0.
			\end{equation*}
			
			Set $$E:=f^*F.$$
			As $X=Z\times B$, the K\"unneth formula yields
			\begin{equation*}
				H^q(X,\operatorname{End}^{0}E)=0
				\quad\text{for every }q.
			\end{equation*}
			In particular, $E$ is simple.
			
			
					\medskip
			We record the cohomology groups needed below.
			A direct calculation from
			\textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[eq:nilpotent-structure]{(\ref*{eq:nilpotent-structure})}} gives
			\begin{equation*}
				\begin{aligned}
					H^2(\mathrm P^\bullet,\partial)
					={}&
					\mathbb C[\alpha_{56}]
					\\
					&\oplus
					\left\langle
					[\alpha_{15}],[\alpha_{16}],
					[\alpha_{25}],[\alpha_{26}]
					\right\rangle
					\\
					&\oplus
					\left\langle
					[\alpha_{45}],[\alpha_{46}]
					\right\rangle
					\\
					&\oplus
					\left\langle
					[\alpha_{13}],[\alpha_{14}],
					[\alpha_{23}],[\alpha_{24}]
					\right\rangle,
				\end{aligned}
			\end{equation*}
			where the four summands have eigenvalues
			$1,\zeta,\zeta^2,\zeta^3$, respectively.
			In degree $3$, all eigenvalues belong to
			$\{\zeta,\zeta^2,\zeta^3,\zeta^4,\zeta^5\}$.
			Taking complex conjugates and invariants therefore gives
			\begin{equation}\label{eq:quotient-O-cohomology}
				H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)
				=
				\mathbb C[\bar\alpha_{56}],
				\quad
				H^3(X,\mathcal O_X)=0.
			\end{equation}
			By \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[direct sum]{(\ref*{direct sum})}}, \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[eq:quotient-O-cohomology]{(\ref*{eq:quotient-O-cohomology})}}
			and the vanishing of $H^q(X,\operatorname{End}^{0}E)$,
			the trace map gives
			\begin{equation*}
				H^2(X,\operatorname{End}E)
				\simeq
				H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)
				\simeq\mathbb C,
				\quad
				H^3(X,\operatorname{End}E)=0.
			\end{equation*}
			
			Let $v_1,\ldots,v_6$ be the holomorphic vector fields
			on $\widetilde X$ dual to
			$\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_6$.
			Their eigenvalues under pull-back are
			$\zeta^{-1},\zeta^{-1},
			\zeta^{-2},\zeta^{-2},1,1$.
			The preceding calculation consequently gives
			\begin{equation*}
				H^2(X,T_X^{1,0})
				=
				\left\langle
				[\bar\alpha_{56}\otimes v_5],\,
				[\bar\alpha_{56}\otimes v_6]
				\right\rangle
				\simeq
				\mathbb C^2.
			\end{equation*}
			
			Consider the connecting map 
			\begin{equation}\label{conne}
				H^1(X,T_X^{1,0})
				\xrightarrow{\;\lrcorner\mathrm{At}(E)\;}
				H^2(X,\operatorname{End}E).
			\end{equation}
			Since $E=f^*F$, we have
			$\operatorname{tr}\mathrm{At}(E)
			=f^*\operatorname{tr}\mathrm{At}(F)$.
			Moreover, $\operatorname{tr}\mathrm{At}(F)$ is a
			nonzero scalar multiple of $c_1(F)$, which is nonzero
			because $\deg F=1$.
			Contracting with $v_6$ and wedging with $\bar\alpha_5$
			therefore gives
			\begin{equation*}
				\operatorname{tr}\left(
				[\bar\alpha_5\otimes v_6]
				\lrcorner\mathrm{At}(E)
				\right)
				=
				c[\bar\alpha_{56}],
				\quad c\neq0.
			\end{equation*}
			Thus the connecting map \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[conne]{(\ref*{conne})}} is nonzero and hence
			surjective, since its target is one-dimensional.
			Together with $H^3(X,\operatorname{End}E)=0$,
			the long exact sequence associated with the Atiyah
			sequence gives
			\begin{equation*}
				H^2(X,A(E))
				\simeq
				H^2(X,T_X^{1,0})
				\simeq
				\mathbb C^2.
			\end{equation*}
			
					\medskip
			Finally, the same exact sequence shows that the tangent
			map of the forgetful morphism has image
			\begin{equation*}
				\operatorname{im}\left(
				H^1(X,A(E))
				\longrightarrow H^1(X,T_X^{1,0})
				\right)
				=
				\ker\bigl(\lrcorner\mathrm{At}(E)\bigr).
			\end{equation*}
			Since \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[conne]{(\ref*{conne})}} is nonzero, this
			tangent map is not surjective.
			Hence the forgetful morphism $\operatorname{Def}(X,E)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Def}(X)$  is not smooth by
			\cite[Corollary  3.6.10]{Man22}.
		\end{enumerate}

body_md:
\label{rem:torsion-canonical}
		It is natural to ask whether Theorem  \ref{main thm2} remains
		true when $K_X$ is merely \emph{torsion}. A natural strategy,
		whether one follows our Tian--Todorov approach or the
		$T^1$-lifting approach of Iacono--Manetti, is to pass to the
		canonical cyclic \'etale cover
		$\pi:\widetilde X\rightarrow X$ as in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[diagram]{(\ref*{diagram})}},
		apply Theorem  \ref{main thm2} to
		$(\widetilde X,\pi^*(\det E))$, and then use
		Lemma  \ref{wells} to descend the vanishing of the obstruction
		classes.
		
				\medskip
		However, even when $X$ is a $\partial\bar\partial$-manifold, it is not clear
		whether $\widetilde X$ is again a $\partial\bar\partial$-manifold. Notice
		that the converse direction holds in much greater
		generality. Indeed, for any surjective morphism
		$f:Y\rightarrow X$ between two equidimensional compact
		complex manifolds, if $Y$ is a $\partial\bar\partial$-manifold, then so is
		$X$; see, e.g.,
		\cite[Theorem  1.1 \& Example  3.1(3)]{Men22}.
		
		This leads to the following:
		\begin{question}
			Let $X$ be an $n$-dimensional compact complex manifold
			with torsion canonical bundle. If $X$ is a
			$\partial\bar\partial$-manifold
			\emph{(resp.\ if $X$ satisfies $\mathbb S^{n,1}$,
				$\mathbb S^{n,2}$ and $\mathbb B^{n-1,2}$)},
			must its canonical cyclic \'etale cover $\widetilde X$
			again be a $\partial\bar\partial$-manifold
			\emph{(resp.\ satisfy $\mathbb S^{n,1}$,
				$\mathbb S^{n,2}$ and $\mathbb B^{n-1,2}$)},
			or can one construct a counterexample to either
			assertion?
		\end{question}

label: step:thomas-curve
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $R'\twoheadrightarrow R$ be a surjection of local Artin
		$\mathbb C$-algebras with kernel $J$, and let $(X_R,E_R)$
		be a given deformation of $(X,E)$ over $R$.
		We will construct a lift of this pair over $R'$.
		The proof is divided into two steps.
		
		\setcounter{step}{0}
		
		\begin{step}{Extend the bundle--curve correspondence.}
			\label{step:thomas-curve}
		\end{step}
		
		We first show that \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[thomas-fixed-correspondence]{(\ref*{thomas-fixed-correspondence})}}
		also holds when $X$ varies:
		\begin{equation}\label{thomas-correspondence}
			\operatorname{Def}(X,E)\cong\operatorname{Def}(X,C).
		\end{equation}
		
		
 Thomas proved the following cohomological identities:
		\begin{equation}\label{thomas-vanishing}
			\begin{gathered}
				h^0(X,V)=1,\quad H^1(X,V)=0,\\
				H^1(X,L^{-1})=H^2(X,L^{-1})=0.
			\end{gathered}
		\end{equation}
		
By \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[1111111]{(\ref*{1111111})}}, the exact sequence in
\cite[Exercise~III. 4.6]{Har77}, applied successively
along small Artin extensions, gives
		\begin{equation}\label{thomas-picard}
			\operatorname{Pic}(X_R)\xrightarrow{\sim}
			\operatorname{Pic}(X).
		\end{equation}
		Thus $\mathcal O_X(-1,1)$ and $L$ extend uniquely up to
		isomorphism to $\mathcal O_{X_R}(-1,1)$ and $L_R$.
		By \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[EEE]{(\ref*{EEE})}}, set
		$V_R:=E_R\otimes\mathcal O_{X_R}(-1,1)$.
		Since $\det V_R$ restricts to $L$,
		\textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[thomas-picard]{(\ref*{thomas-picard})}} gives $\det V_R\cong L_R$.
		
		
		\medskip
		The equality $H^1(X,V)=0$ allows $s$ to extend to $s_R$.
		Together with $H^0(X,V)=\mathbb C s$, this gives
		$$
		H^0(X_R,V_R)=R\,s_R,\quad s_R|_X=s.
		$$
		Any other extension of $s$ is therefore $u s_R$
		for an invertible element $u\in R$.
		Since $Z(u s_R)=Z(s_R)$, the closed subspace
		$C_R:=Z(s_R)$ is independent of this choice.
		Moreover, $s$ cuts out $C$ in codimension two,
		so $C_R$ is a flat deformation of $C$.
		Hence the given bundle $E_R$ determines $C_R\subset X_R$.
		
				\medskip
		Conversely, suppose that $C_R\subset X_R$ is given.
		Both $\det N_{C_R/X_R}$ and $L_R|_{C_R}$ extend $L|_C$.
		Since $H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)=0$, the same uniqueness
		argument as in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[thomas-picard]{(\ref*{thomas-picard})}} gives
		$$
		\det N_{C_R/X_R}\cong L_R|_{C_R}.
		$$
		The vanishings for $L^{-1}$ in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[thomas-vanishing]{(\ref*{thomas-vanishing})}}
		also hold for $L_R^{-1}$.
		The Serre construction of \cite[\S 3]{Tho99}
		therefore applies over $R$:
		$H^2(X_R,L_R^{-1})=0$ gives a rank-two bundle $V_R$
		in the sequence \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[thomas-serre]{(\ref*{thomas-serre})}} over $R$, and
		$H^1(X_R,L_R^{-1})=0$ makes it unique up to isomorphism.
		Twisting by $\mathcal O_{X_R}(1,-1)$ as in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[EEE]{(\ref*{EEE})}}
		recovers $E_R$. This proves \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[thomas-correspondence]{(\ref*{thomas-correspondence})}}.
		
		\begin{step}{Lift the curve and the threefold.}
			\label{step:thomas-lift}
		\end{step}
		
		By \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[thomas-correspondence]{(\ref*{thomas-correspondence})}}, it remains to lift
		$(X_R,C_R)$.
		
		By \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[thomas-picard]{(\ref*{thomas-picard})}}, the line bundles
		$\mathcal O_X(1,0)$ and $\mathcal O_X(0,1)$ extend to $X_R$.
		Moreover, \cite[Equation (3.2) with
		$(k,l)=(1,0)$ \& $(0,1)$]{Tho99}, gives
		$$
		H^1(X,\mathcal O_X(1,0))
		=
		H^1(X,\mathcal O_X(0,1))
		=0.
		$$
		Thus the coordinate sections $x,y,z$ and $u,v,w$
		extend and still generate these line bundles.
		They define a morphism
		$$
		X_R\longrightarrow P_R:=P\times\operatorname{Spec}R
		$$
		extending $X\subset P$,  which remains a closed
		immersion by Nakayama's lemma.
		Since $X_R$ is flat over $R$ and $X\subset P$ is
		a hypersurface, the immersion $X_R\subset P_R$ is
		regular of codimension one
		\cite[Proposition~D.2.5]{Ser06}.
		Its ideal is therefore a line bundle extending
		$\mathcal O_P(-3,-3)$. 
		As $H^1(P,\mathcal O_P)=0$, the same uniqueness argument
		as in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[thomas-picard]{(\ref*{thomas-picard})}} identifies this ideal with
		$\mathcal O_{P_R}(-3,-3)$.
		Hence
		$$
		X_R=\{F_R=0\}\subset P_R
		$$
		for a bicubic polynomial $F_R$ lifting $F$.
		
		\medskip
		In the Addendum to the revised version of \cite{Tho99},
		Thomas described the deformations of $C$ inside $P$
		as a moving line in the first factor together with
		a moving point in the second.
		Writing $\mathfrak m_R$ for the maximal ideal of $R$,
		his description gives
		\begin{equation}\label{thomas-embedded-pair}
			C_R=\{x=ay+bz,\ u=cw,\ v=dw\}
			\subset\{F_R=0\},
			\quad a,b,c,d\in\mathfrak m_R.
		\end{equation}
		
		
				\medskip
		Choose lifts $\widetilde a,\widetilde b,\widetilde c,
		\widetilde d$ to $R'$.
		The same equations define
		$$
		C_{R'}:=
		\{x=\widetilde a y+\widetilde b z,\
		u=\widetilde c w,\
		v=\widetilde d w\}
		\cong\mathbb P^1_{R'}
		$$
		inside $P_{R'}:=P\times\operatorname{Spec}R'$.
		Thus $C_{R'}$ is a flat lift of $C_R$.
		Choose also a bicubic lift $\widetilde F$ of $F_R$ and set
		$$
		Q(y,z):=
		\widetilde F
		\bigl(\widetilde a y+\widetilde b z,\ y,\ z;\
		\widetilde c,\ \widetilde d,\ 1\bigr).
		$$
		The containment in \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[thomas-embedded-pair]{(\ref*{thomas-embedded-pair})}} implies
		that every coefficient of the homogeneous cubic $Q$
		lies in $J$.
		Since $\widetilde F$ has degree three in $u,v,w$,
		$$
		\widetilde F|_{C_{R'}}=w^3Q(y,z).
		$$
		We therefore set
		\begin{equation}\label{thomas-correction}
			F_{R'}:=\widetilde F-w^3Q(y,z).
		\end{equation}
		The correction is again bicubic, and
		\textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[thomas-correction]{(\ref*{thomas-correction})}} gives
		\begin{equation}\label{thomas-lifting}
			F_{R'}\bmod J=F_R,
			\quad
			F_{R'}|_{C_{R'}}=0.
		\end{equation}
		
				\medskip
		Put $X_{R'}:=\{F_{R'}=0\}\subset P_{R'}$.
		Since its central fibre $X$ is a smooth hypersurface,
		the Jacobian criterion shows that $X_{R'}$ is smooth,
		hence flat, over $R'$.
		Thus \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[thomas-lifting]{(\ref*{thomas-lifting})}} gives a lift
		$(X_{R'},C_{R'})$ of $(X_R,C_R)$.
		By \textcolor{Red2}{\hyperref[thomas-correspondence]{(\ref*{thomas-correspondence})}}, this lifted pair
		determines a bundle $E_{R'}$ restricting to $E_R$.
		This proves that $\operatorname{Def}(X,E)$ is smooth.
